blocks.1: This is not material I have found by researching archives or other written sources. It is just a little about how I remember the war from my childhood, mixed with things I have heard told since.
blocks.2: There were no Germans permanently stationed in Eivindvik for long periods, but we nevertheless had quite a lot of contact with the occupiers. They came here on raids and house searches, and German boats often lay here. Boats that stayed for a while were usually camouflaged with bushes and scrub. We children thought this was a little exciting. Sometimes the warships fired at English planes flying over here. I remember we saw the tracer fire like shooting stars across the sky, but we never saw the planes hit. German fighter planes often flew low over the village, between the mountains. Once we saw two German planes chasing an English one. The Englishman dived straight down along Mikkelfjellet; it almost looked as if the plane would go straight into the ground, but it pulled up again in towards Dalen. The Germans followed, and all three planes disappeared over the mountain at Hansslettet.
blocks.4: One fine winter's day the boat “Blåveis” was sunk by English planes in Stemnebøosen. We were in Dalen to fetch wood that day. A lot of fresh snow had fallen, and all the neighbours were together clearing the road with the horses. From Kvilesteinen we saw the English planes dive down, and we heard the bursts of fire. One of the planes came a little ahead of the others; it seemed that the leader of the operation sat in it, and when he dived, the others dived after. They made several attacks before the boat was sunk.
blocks.5: Alf Sæternes has told me that “Blåveis” had earlier been Christian Michelsen's pleasure yacht. The boat was later raised and repaired. She was named “Solbris”, and it was this boat that the prisoners convicted of treason at Ulven used when they escaped to Argentina after the war.
blocks.7: Late one autumn (I think it was in 1944) the old “Gula” was attacked by English planes in Nyhamarsundet. At home we saw the planes come like big birds over Mikkelfjellet (we saw them before we heard the sound), turn and disappear again for new attacks. This was repeated several times. Two of the passengers on board “Gula” lost their lives and several were wounded. The boat was badly damaged. Everyone wondered why “Gula” should be torpedoed; most thought it must have been a case of mistaken identity on the part of the English.
blocks.8: Another boat was involved in the attack, a cargo boat, and there one of the crew was killed and several wounded. Perhaps it was this boat the airmen were after?
blocks.9: The most likely reason for the attack on the two boats was probably that they happened to be in Nyhamarsundet when the planes came over that day. English planes often made sorties along the Norwegian coast and attacked freight boats to make transport unsafe and difficult for the occupying power. They were also after the German patrol boats operating along the coast.
blocks.10: Olav Dingen, who later lived in the house up on “the farm” at Haugane, worked for a long time as crew with Fylkesbaatane, and he was on board “Gula” when this attack happened.
blocks.12: My strongest memories of the war, however, are from the April days of 1940. I still remember well the sad mood when Ole Midtun, among the first to be called up for military service, left on the evening of Tuesday 9 April. He knew nothing about there being war in the country until he came home from the outfields with sheep at dusk and had to get ready to leave in a great hurry. He just had time for a trip to the quay to fetch a few sacks of flour for his parents before he set off. Erling Korsvold and Lars Svaberg were in the same call-up. The lads travelled, together with many others from Gulen, on “Kommandøren” up the Sognefjord to Gudvangen. From there they walked most of the way to Voss and were taken on to the fighting in Valdres.
blocks.13: About 14 days or so later the mood was just as sad; there was a new call-up, and from the village here Gunnar Henriksbø went then. This time too the soldiers were taken up the Sognefjord on “Kommandøren”. On the way the boat was bombed by German planes. At Leikanger bombs also fell on land and exploded in people's gardens. “Kommandøren” was not hit, but the skipper on board was struck by a bomb splinter and had to go to hospital in Lærdal. At Leikanger they got word that the war in southern Norway was over, and after spending the night at Kaupanger they went home. It was sad when the lads left, but all the greater joy when they came back; we looked up to them as heroes. Erling Korsvold got a German bullet through one arm. He was the only one of the lads from here who was wounded.
blocks.15: When war broke out, some of the men in the village were issued rifles. There was also at least one machine gun here. I remember that it stood at our house, and it was Gunnar Henriksbø (before he was called up) and Arne Fosse who were responsible for it. Gunnar was working for us at the time. Villagers were ordered to stand guard. There was an armed guard at the telephone cable on Gulløyna, and likewise on the steamer quay.
blocks.16: On the first day of the war a Norwegian military plane with two men on board came here. It was said they had been in combat out in Mjømnesundet. I have never found out why the plane landed and stayed here. Those of the villagers who helped tow it into place, hide and camouflage it, were told nothing about the reason. The plane lay by the shore roughly where Dr Normann's boathouse now stands. Later it was moved into Midtunvågen, and after a while it flew away. This plane was probably part of the Sognefjord air group, one of several air groups set up under the command of Captain Manshaus. The Sognefjord air group had its headquarters at Balestrand (later Vetlefjorden) and temporary stations at Eivindvik and Sogndal.
blocks.17: In the April days a cargo boat, “Vard” of Haugesund, also lay in Midtunvågen. She lay by the shore inside the boathouse belonging to the people at Haugane. She was camouflaged and well hidden. Later she was moved out to Hjartåsvågen. It was said that the boat was loaded with cabbage. Olav H. Tveit says he was there when the boat was moved from Midtunvågen to Hjartåsvågen.
blocks.19: Shortly before the fighting in Western Norway was over, there was a skirmish between German and Norwegian marines out at Grønevika. One of the Norwegian marines there was Gustav Mulelid from Florø. Later in the war he went over to England and joined the Norwegian forces there. After the war he went to sea with Captain Olav Midthun. What I write here about this attack is based on information from Mulelid, passed on by Olav Midthun, notes from the book “Norges sjøkrig 1940–45” (Norway's naval war 1940–45) by Commander Steen, and information from villagers who remember this event in 1940.
blocks.20: The Norwegian soldiers had been in combat at Horten. After the area around the Oslofjord had been occupied, they had made their way over to Sogn and came out of the Sognefjord on a boat called “Steinar”. The boat lay here and is mentioned in Steen's book as “the guard smack”. The commander on board was L.H. Henriksen.
blocks.21: On 30 April two Norwegian minelayers, which had been taken over by the Germans on 9 April, sailed north from Bergen with German crews. The boats were called “Tyr” and “Uller”. Their task was to lay mines in two lines between Losna and Rutletangane. On reports from the sheriffs in Lindås and Eivindvik and from the coastguard station on Byrknesøy, the commander of the air groups, Captain Manshaus, was informed of the voyage, and planes from Vetlefjorden attacked the boats west of Skjerjehamn at about half past seven in the evening. The boats took no direct bomb hits, but on “Uller” 3 men were wounded. The Norwegian planes were not damaged by the fire from the vessels. The boats continued north, and a little later they began laying mines across the Sognefjord.
blocks.22: Later that night they were bombed again by a Norwegian Heinkel plane from Vetlefjorden, and “Uller” was so badly damaged that the Germans beached her on the south of Losna. This time too the plane was not damaged. “Tyr” took the soldiers off “Uller” and set course south towards Bergen. Henriksen on “Steinar” was ordered to attack when “Tyr” passed Eivindvik. He and his men made their way out to Grønevik. They connected to the telephone line above the Grønevik farm and were in contact with the neutrality guard at Riseneset.
blocks.23: The idea was to get a patrol over to Hisarøy, so that the Germans would come under crossfire, but they had to give that up when the German boat came up on them so quickly.
blocks.24: Before the attack the people at Grønevika had to be warned so that they could get to a safer place. The man of the house, Lars, was ill at the time, and he was carried out to the cowshed.
blocks.25: The attack took place early in the morning. It was clear and calm. Steen's book says, among other things, that “the deck was full of men standing smoking and chatting, apparently suspecting nothing”, and when the Norwegians opened fire “the machine guns raked the vessel from stem to stern with good effect”, and further that “the Germans were so surprised by the sudden fire that they only had time to fire a few rounds with automatic weapons at the machine-gun positions on land before the vessel had passed them on its way south”. The German fire did no other damage than to set the heather alight in the parsonage outfield, and the fire was put out during the day by villagers who came to help. The book also says that many Germans were killed and wounded; among other things a lieutenant on the bridge was hit and bled so heavily that “die ganze Brücke schwimmt von Blut” (the whole bridge is swimming in blood). This may have been the reason for what people here tell, that the boat made a wide turn and nearly ran aground at Tangen. From Lindås it was reported that “Tyr” passed southwards with her flag at half-mast.
blocks.26: People in the village were also told that an attack was to take place, and they quickly gathered with what weapons they had. The doctor's boat, “GåPå”, was to take them out, but before they got away word came that it was all over. Gunnar Henriksbø, who was there himself, has told this, but I cannot say for certain whether it applied to everyone from the village. Gustav Mulelid cannot remember anyone from the village taking part, so probably no one from here was in the attack itself.
blocks.27: After the fight the Norwegian soldiers, once they had got supplies from the Sandal shop, went out towards Nåra. There they meant to set up a position facing the Sogn Sea, but immediately afterwards went north to take part in the fighting there, as the area here was surrendered to the Germans. When the fighting in the north was over too, they came south again with “Steinar”.
blocks.28: Two German boats have been mentioned in connection with the attack at Grønevik, but everything suggests that only one of them was in Folefotsundet when the attack took place.
blocks.30: After this attack people were afraid the Germans would take revenge on the village by military action, as they were said to have threatened. The people at Grønevik stayed away from home for a few days, and from the area out by the steamer quay many “evacuated” into Midtunvågen, some even into Midtundalen, and the parsonage hut by Svartevatnet was also used as a refuge.
blocks.31: The sight of this “migration of peoples”, and the tension among the people in those days, is firmly fixed in my memory.
blocks.32: Some think they remember German planes over the village the day after the attack, but no “revenge attack” came. Some also say that the German boat fortunately did not reach Bergen but was sunk on the way, and believe this was why we escaped reprisals.
blocks.33: Perhaps the reason was rather that the fighting in our part of the country ended so soon afterwards?
blocks.34: This incident out at Grønevika is said to be described in several books on the war in Norway 1940–45.
blocks.36: The resistance movement that grew up in our country after the capitulation in 1940 spread here too. There were many good “jøssings” (patriots) here, but I do not know much about what went on. Children were to know as little as possible. It was only after the war was over that we learned something of what had gone on. The district doctor Hallvard Natvik, who just before he came here had served as a doctor during the fighting in the April days, was an active resistance man in several fields. Among other things he and his boatman, John Hellesund, helped transport people on secret missions. It is told that once when Natvik came from Solund on such an errand – he was then the only crew on the boat, but had two resistance men in the cabin – his engine stopped on the Sogn Sea. He was not very good with engines and had trouble getting it started again. On a German boat that came past they saw something was wrong and offered help. The German engineer came aboard and got the engine going. Natvik thanked them very much for the help, the Germans left the boat, and the rest of the trip went fine.
blocks.37: Another who did what he could to hinder the occupiers was the sheriff, Jakob Eikenes. He and the smith Toralf Sande were the only ones here in Eivindvik taken by the Germans. Eikenes was taken to Germany, while Sande was held prisoner at Espeland near Bergen. I think Eikenes was arrested in 1943 and Sande early in 1945. Both came out of captivity without visible harm. They were received with great relief and joy when they again set foot on home soil.
blocks.38: The winter of 1944/45 must have been a hard time for Lydia Sande. At the end of August 1944 her eldest son, aged 10, drowned in the sound just outside their home, and a few months later her husband was arrested by the Germans.
blocks.39: Like several others in the village, Sande had bought one of the flagpoles used at the Gulating gathering in the grove in 1938. The flagpole had not been finished and raised before the war came, but in the days of peace in 1945 some young people got together and put the flagpole up, so that when Sande came home from captivity he was greeted with the flag hoisted.
blocks.40: In addition to all weapons, the radio sets were also confiscated by the occupying power, but many had hidden away both rifles and radios. In secret people listened to broadcasts from England and spread news of how the war was going in Europe. On the whole people knew how things stood at any given time.
blocks.41: The Germans often carried out raids to search for radios and any weapons. On one such occasion it was quite exciting for Mons Skauge in Fonnevika. He had a radio receiver in the barn, hidden in the hay. The Germans had probably been tipped off about this; they came and prodded with hayforks all around where the set stood, but did not find it. I have heard that they found the cardboard box the set had come in, and that it showed what type of set Skauge had. He had handed in an old, useless set. The Germans now wanted to go and check in the store of handed-in radios whether Skauge's set was there. The confiscated sets were stored at the parsonage behind a sealed lock, and the key to the store was at the sheriff's office. On the day of the raid it so happened that the sheriff was not at home, and the deputy, Olav Bøe, who was also a good “jøssing”, “assured” them that it was the sheriff personally who had the key and that he as deputy could not get in there now, but it could be arranged “tomorrow”, for then the sheriff would be back. The Germans fell for this, and during the night the radio sets were swapped, so that everything was in order the next day.
blocks.42: Toralf Sande was also subjected to a similar house search. He had apparently hidden the radio in the potato cellar, and the Germans did not find it. It was said that after the search he kept the set hidden in the church for a short time until he found a new hiding place. He lived near the church and was for a time church caretaker and gravedigger.
blocks.44: I remember well that one day a group of us children, climbing in Storurda, came across a rifle lying under a stone. I think it was a shotgun. It must have been a villager who had hidden it there. He must have found out that we had seen it, for when we came back up a little later the gun was gone.
blocks.45: The Germans sometimes searched scree slopes and other possible hiding places in the outfields, looking for weapons and radio receivers, perhaps also transmitters; they even went right into Midtundalen and checked the huts, but I have not heard of them finding anything here.
blocks.46: Once when they were searching the scree at Jytten, above Gryta, and took a break in the middle of it, one of them sang and yodelled in true Tyrolean style so that it echoed across the village. It was actually very beautiful; he was a good singer.
blocks.47: There were many German soldiers at the fortifications at Risenes and Rutledal, and they sometimes came round the farms here wanting to buy butter, meat and other food. They surely did not get much.
blocks.48: The farmers were required to make compulsory deliveries of almost every kind of farm produce. Once the farmers at Midtun were ordered to make an extra compulsory delivery of pine logs from the plantation. These were to be used as sleepers under railway lines.
blocks.49: In addition to all kinds of farm produce, the Germans also needed draught power, so some, mostly the small farms, even had to hand over their horses. One smallholder here took it particularly hard when they took his horse. He was a warm friend of animals and found it so hard to part with his horse that he considered putting the animal down so that it would not fall into the hands of the Germans. But the horse was fetched. It was a fine horse; those who received it praised the animal highly. The man was hard up, but he would not accept the money he was given for his fine horse. It was put in the bank, and I do not know what happened to it after that.
blocks.50: This man kept a rifle in his house, and once when two Germans walked across his property he fetched the rifle and wanted to shoot them. It took real force to stop him, it is said.
blocks.51: There were restrictions and orders in every direction. As soon as darkness came in the evening the blackout curtains had to be drawn. Everything was to be blacked out so that any English airmen would get no help of any kind with navigation. The newspapers were censored and full of German propaganda, and the news reports were twisted, but those that came from England through the hidden radio receivers were genuine.
blocks.52: Everyone who was to travel, even just to Bergen, had to have a travel permit and a pass. Those who fished also had to have a permit for that. The permits were issued at the sheriff's office. At the supplies board we got ration cards. As far as I remember, all everyday goods were rationed, and the substitute goods we got were very poor; the soaps, for example, which were called “B-soaps”, were very hard to get any lather from at all. The coffee substitute was also very poor stuff. One got shoes of fish skin. There was little of all foodstuffs. People used natural resources as best they could. In autumn the hillsides were full of berry pickers. Even most of those who were not farmers kept pigs and hens; they fitted out rooms for them in cellars, tool sheds and storehouses, and many kept rabbits.
blocks.53: During the war there were warm, fruitful summers but severe winters. At a barn fire at Henriksbø in January 1942 it was impossible to fight the fire because the big river was frozen to the bottom.
blocks.54: In summer during the war years there were many townspeople in the village. Many had family here, but others were also taken in so that they could get out of the city for a few weeks. Schoolchildren from the city were placed around the farms during the holidays to have a stay “in the country”. These children usually, like the children here, took part in the work on the farms, and they seemed to settle in well in village life. Most of them probably also put on a few extra welcome kilos, hard times notwithstanding, before going back to the city in the autumn.
blocks.56: Businesses that flourished in wartime were the clog factories. Clogs were used in every house. When people were indoors, the pairs of clogs stood in rows in porches and hallways. The clogs were warm and good, but could be slippery when the sole was worn. With worn-down heels they were excellent for sliding on patches of ice and hard-frozen ground. The speed could get quite high, but it was not always easy to steer properly and stop in time; we often got black and blue.
blocks.57: The clogs were lacquered on the outside so that they would not soak up water. The lacquer was, as I remember, always black. At the clog factory in Sellevåg the floor of the lacquering loft was completely black from drops of lacquer that fell during the lacquering work. This work was done with an ordinary brush.
blocks.58: Clogs and boots with wooden soles were also much used. Sometimes fish skin was used instead of leather for the uppers of the clogs and boots.
blocks.60: During the war Norwegians were forbidden to gather for dancing. One Saturday evening I remember that we children at least were very excited. For some time a number of German soldiers had been, and still were, quartered in the community hall. They played and shouted and were clearly having a great time on the space in front of the hall in the evening. The young people of the village gathered for a dance, with accordion music, in Ole Midtun's barn. When the music and noise of the dancing streamed out of the barn, it went completely quiet at the community hall. We sat a little way from the barn and watched excitedly, but nothing happened; the German soldiers kept quiet. The young people also danced in the community hall when circumstances allowed.
blocks.61: After Eikenes was taken by the Germans and Bøe had resigned as deputy, a Nazi sheriff and a new deputy came here. They were actually moderate in their duties. It is told that once when the young people were dancing in the community hall, the sheriff had a visit from a higher-ranking Nazi. The man wanted to go to the meeting hall to see whether there was dancing. The sheriff is said to have prevented this by assuring him that he had already sent his deputy there. The deputy was there all right. He had his accordion with him, and it was he who provided the dance music.
blocks.62: A really big illegal event during the war, which lit up the grey existence and which everyone who was there (and that was nearly everyone in the whole village) will surely remember, was when we celebrated the 17th of May in Midtundalen in 1942, but I have mentioned that elsewhere in these writings, in the section on other customs.
blocks.63: Right at the end of the war – it was a Sunday evening – a German warship lay at the steamer quay. Two young men were sent away from the quay area by the Germans. They then went up Flolidfjellet with a strong torch and began to “signal” out towards the islands and the sea. Whether it was the “signalling” that did it I do not know, but the German boat cast off and left the area.
blocks.64: In the last months of the war we once saw a plane circling at a very great height. It looked as if the pilot felt sure he was out of range of German defensive weapons and amused himself by making “curlicues” with the white trail of smoke the plane left behind. Some believed they could read from the shape of the trail that it was a greeting from King Haakon VII, who was then in London. This must probably have been one of the Allies' earliest types of jet aircraft.
blocks.65: There were often planes over the village in the war years. One night in the last winter of the war there was particularly much air activity. We understood that something special was happening, and in the days after we heard that several containers of food and other provisions had been dropped in Dalsbygda. This was after the build-up of the Bjørn West forces in the Masfjord mountains had begun, and the goods were supplies for these forces, but were dropped in the wrong place by the English.
blocks.66: Nazis lived in the cabin on Timrøyna during parts of the war. We always thought it a little creepy with those Nazis over there and kept wondering what they were plotting. One of them, the one who then owned the island, was, from what I have heard, arrested there by Norwegian police in the days of peace in May 1945. He was among those who later escaped from captivity at Ulven near Bergen to Argentina on M/B “Solbris”. The local history of Gulen tells about this.
blocks.67: One of the boats Johannes Nygård now owns, M/B “Motig”, was used in the England traffic (the “Shetland bus”) during the war. This was the first boat that Shetlands-Larsen took across the North Sea. She was much used for transport between Shetland and Scotland.
blocks.68: The war years were a difficult time; people lived under fear and coercion, and there was enormous relief when Germany capitulated. People cheered and sang, fired salutes with whatever explosives they had, brought out the fine, clean Norwegian cross flag, let their national feelings loose; the joy of freedom was overwhelming. No one who experienced 8 May 1945 will forget it. People here gathered in the community hall, where, through a radio set that had escaped the German order to hand them in, we had the joyful news confirmed and shared in the mood. People floated on happiness in the days that followed. There was life, bustle and festivity everywhere in those warm, light, fine spring days and nights, and a heartfelt, great and deep gratitude spread to all who had fought so hard, and especially to those who had given their lives so that we could once again experience freedom, and such unforgettable days.
blocks.69: Among those who gave everything were two men from our village who had moved away, the brothers Johan and Hjørleiv Midttun (Henriksbø). Johan was arrested by the Germans on 15 March 1941 and was shot at Akershus on 4 December the same year. Hjørleiv was a radio operator and was lost when “Kosmos II” was torpedoed on 28 October 1942.
blocks.70: In the lower churchyard, south-east of Lovseieberget, there used to be a large grave called “The English grave”. In it, as far as people now remember, 16 English soldiers lost in the First World War were buried. These soldiers were, from what I have been told, found at the entrance to the Sognefjord, some at Lihellene, and otherwise in the area out by Hisarøy.
blocks.71: A large stone pillar with an inscription was raised on the grave, and around it were smaller stones with chains between them. Several people also remember that there were several smaller gravestones (probably 4) within the enclosed area. At the peace after the Second World War in 1945, I remember that “the old sheriff”, Bredvik, gave a speech at this grave and praised the British nation for its efforts in the Second World War too. Sheriff Eikenes had not yet come back from German captivity, and Bredvik served as sheriff for a short time that spring of peace.
blocks.72: Later English war graves were gathered in larger cemeteries. The grave here was dug up and the remains taken to a cemetery in Fredrikstad in 1961. The stone pillar and the other stones were removed at the same time, but a small stone has been put back with a copper plate which, in English, says that the grave has been moved to Fredrikstad. This stone stands east of a footpath across the churchyard. Several of us think we remember that the memorial stone over “The English grave” stood on the west side of this footpath.
blocks.73: In the Second World War, at the end of 1944, an English combat plane flew straight into a mountainside on Losna. Einar Navdal (farm no. 15, holding no. 6) was there when the remains of the crew were brought down. He has told that they had to use ropes to get down to the plane, which stood with half its body stuck in the mountain. Remains of both the men and the plane lay scattered over a large area. They believed there had been 3 soldiers in the plane. They were buried by the church here, but these graves too were moved away at the same time as the large English grave was removed.
